The project aims to make the analysis of cognitive interviews more efficient by combining human expertise with innovative AI-based coding methods, thereby extending the reach of the method. In addition, the project contributes to understanding how children and parents assess children’s health in large-scale studies. For this purpose, potential differences in health assessment strategies between the respondent groups are examined, and systematic variations by age and gender are identified.

Background
To ensure the quality of survey research, survey instruments are validated using both qualitative and quantitative methods. Both approaches, however, come with limitations. While quantitative analyses can reveal efficiently generalizable relationships between different concepts and systematic differences between respondents due to large sample sizes, they are limited in their ability to capture complex cognitive processes within individuals.
In contrast to quantitative methods, qualitative approaches such as semi-structured cognitive interviews provide deeper insights into participants’ thought patterns. However, the high cost of such studies often limits sample size and scalability, which affects general validity, generalizability, and the ability to account for differences between subgroups.
Integrating the strengths of both methods can significantly improve survey research by enabling a holistic understanding of phenomena while simultaneously leveraging the benefits of quantitative validation. However, combining both approaches presents a challenge.
The AI-SIC project contributes by developing an AI-based approach for semi-automatic coding using an active learning strategy. This involves combining machine coding algorithms with human coding skills. Furthermore, new methods are applied to efficiently and thoroughly validate survey instruments in order to address research gaps concerning the already established measurement of self-rated health. This will help to close the gap between qualitative and quantitative methods and answer open questions about how children and their parents assess the health of children.

Approach and Methods
The project is divided into four substantive work packages.
The first work package “Development of the semi-automatic coding framework InTraCo” (Dr. Andreas Niekler & Stephan Poppe; University of Leipzig) aims to methodologically and technically integrate language-based machine learning and reliable semi-automatic coding procedures into the toolbox of computer-assisted social sciences. The goal is to combine machine coding algorithms with human inductive coding skills to increase efficiency in coding extensive qualitative interview data.
The second work package “Application and Evaluation of InTraCo” (Dr. Andreas Niekler & Stephan Poppe; University of Leipzig) is dedicated to the application of the newly developed approach as well as its validation and adaptation.
The third work package “Exploring the self- and proxy-assessment strategies of children and parents” (Dr. Jacqueline Kroh; LIfBi) utilizes the highly complex data obtained and examines whether the new method can provide added value for content-related analyses using machine learning procedures. This is intended to gain a more comprehensive understanding of how both children and parents assess children’s health.
The fourth work package “Comparability of assessment strategies and results between self- and proxy-assessments of children and parents” (Prof. Dr. Julia Offenhammer-Tuppat; University of Leipzig) deepens the insights gained in work package three and investigates similarities and differences between various respondent groups in the children’s self-assessments and the parents’ proxy assessments of child health.

Data Collection
AI-SIC uses qualitative data and conducts cognitive interviews based on web-based as well as real face-to-face interviews.

title: Silicon Interviews: A Two-Agent Interview Simulation
text:
Planned talk for the ESRA Conference. Shortly, we will publish an article related to our research. For now, you can find the abstract of the talk here.

Abstract
Selecting an appropriate measurement instrument in social science survey research presents researchers with a fundamental trade-off between depth and scalability. The emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs), with their diverse applications and enhanced user-friendliness, opens new possibilities for social science research methodology. While recent research has primarily focused on whether LLMs can replace human respondents through so-called silicon samples, less attention has been paid to their potential to also replace interviewers. Early findings suggest that AI interviewers can surpass humans in specific tasks, such as active listening, while also reducing biases resulting from reactivity and social desirability effects, but their capabilities remain underexplored.
Our study takes a novel approach: simulating AI-AI interactions, where LLMs act as both interviewers and respondents in semi-structured interview settings. This dual-simulation framework enables us to rigorously test and refine interviewing methodologies while addressing the dynamic nature of human interactions, which are inherently unpredictable and context-dependent. As a test case, we simulate interviews with children—a particularly challenging context that demands empathetic and adaptive interviewing techniques. By adhering to established guidelines for interviewing children, we evaluate LLMs on their ability to generate dynamic follow-up questions, maintain conversational flow, and exhibit algorithmic fidelity in both roles, modeling complex human interactions.
Beyond addressing common methodological challenges, such as social desirability biases and subjective inconsistencies, our framework offers a scalable solution for testing and refining interview methodologies. Generating ‘silicon interviews’, enables the development and refinement of downstream tasks, such as computational coding and analysis, by providing more robust large-scale datasets. Our findings underscore the potential of AI-driven simulations to advance survey research by bridging methodological gaps, reducing costs, and enhancing the scalability of interview-based research, thereby easing the trade-off between large-scale surveys and semi-structured interviews.

title: Evaluating Active Learning Setups for Qualitative Interview Coding
text:
After completing our preliminary work on transcription, we can now shift focus to the next task: coding our interviews. The aim is to assign labels to interview segments that reflect our dimensions of interest. To align our methodological approach with the needs of our sociological researchers, we decided to use active learning for the labeling process.
Active learning enables human intervention during coding while simultaneously training a machine learning model. Over time, this model can support – and potentially partially automate – the coding process. In this short research notice, we present our findings on different active learning configurations and explain how we identified a suitable setup for our use case.

title: Evaluating Active Learning Setups for Qualitative Interview Coding
text:

The aim is to assign labels to interview segments that reflect our dimensions of interest. To align our methodological approach with the needs of our sociological researchers, we decided to use active learning for the labeling process.
Active learning enables human intervention during coding while simultaneously training a machine learning model. In this short research notice, we present our findings on different active learning configurations and explain how we identified a suitable setup for our use case.

title: Evaluating Active Learning Setups for Qualitative Interview Coding
text:
Test Setting
Active learning refers to an iterative learning setup in which an ML model is trained repeatedly. In each iteration, annotators label examples that are expected to be particularly informative for deciding whether a given label should be assigned. The model is then retrained, and a new batch of examples is selected. The overarching goal is to minimize the total number of labeled examples required.
We implemented our experiments using the small-text active learning framework in Python, which offers a wide range of configuration options.

Data, Annotation, and Evaluation Strategy
Before involving expert coders in annotating the final interview data, we conducted experiments on synthetic interviews to establish baseline practices. These interviews were generated in an AI-to-AI interview setting, where roles, socio-demographic characteristics, and interview guidelines were provided as context.1
From these interviews, we constructed training and test splits. For coding, we selected a small subset of codes that had already been used in a previous study by our team Kroh u. a. (2023).
During data preparation, it became clear that inter-coder agreement would be a central concern for evaluating model performance. A key question is whether a model trained on data labeled by one coder can be meaningfully evaluated on data labeled by another, especially if their interpretations of the codes differ. Even within annotations produced by the same coder, consistency cannot be taken for granted: perceptions of concepts may evolve during the labeling process, and subtle textual differences can lead to different label assignments.
To allow for later analysis of these effects, we tracked which coder labeled each example. For the experiments reported here, we restricted evaluation to a smaller subset of the test data annotated by a single coder, providing a more stable reference point.


Model Architecture and Active Learning Configuration
Turning to the technical setup, our task involves extracting nuanced information from natural language, making transformer-based models a natural choice. Within small-text, two transformer-based approaches are available: a token-level transformer integration (TransformerBasedClassificationFactory) and sentence transformers trained using the SetFit paradigm (SetFitClassificationFactory).
Our experiments focus on sentence transformers, as prior work suggests they outperform the token-based approach in low-data scenarios Tunstall u. a. (2022). Nevertheless, we included one standard transformer model for comparison. Since each interview segment may receive multiple codes, the task is formulated as a multi-label classification problem.
In addition to text representation, several configuration choices can influence model performance. Each model requires a classification head to map embeddings to label predictions. The default option is a logistic regression head implemented in sklearn. As an alternative, we evaluated a differentiable classification head implemented as a linear layer in torch. This option allows for end-to-end training of both the embedding model and the classifier and would later enable the computation of integrated gradients for token-level attribution scores.
For the differentiable head, we tested both full end-to-end training and a setup where embeddings were kept fixed and only the head was trained. Finally, we varied the query strategy that determines which samples are selected for annotation. We compared a prediction-entropy (PE) baseline with the more suitable CategoryVectorInconsistencyAndRanking (CVIAR) strategy, which is designed specifically for multi-label scenarios.
For each configuration, we simulated an active learning run by initializing the model with 20 labeled examples, followed by five iterations in which 25 additional examples were annotated. This resulted in 145 labeled samples per run. The total labeled data pool contained 210 examples, with each configuration selecting different subsets depending on model and query strategy.
We used MLflow to log model configurations, evaluation metrics, training times, and sample selection across iterations. All experiments were run on a SLURM cluster using four Tesla A100 GPUs with 32 GB of memory each, although substantially fewer resources are sufficient when running active learning in a fixed configuration.

title: Evaluating Active Learning Setups for Qualitative Interview Coding
text:
Results
A clear pattern emerges from the results: configurations using a differentiable classification head perform substantially worse than those using a logistic regression head. This is most likely due to the small number of training examples available. Since such low-data conditions are typical in qualitative coding tasks, this finding suggests that differentiable heads are not well suited for our intended application.
Figure 1 summarizes the performance of models using a differentiable head, while Figure 2 shows results for models with a logistic regression head. Performance is evaluated using the macro-averaged F1 score, which balances precision and recall across all codes.
Across almost all settings, the MiniLM model outperforms the newer e5 models – even when compared to the much larger 0.3B-parameter “Medium” variant. The choice of query strategy also has a consistent effect: CategoryVectorInconsistencyAndRanking outperforms entropy-based sampling in nearly every configuration.
Interestingly, the baseline model performed reasonably well against the SetFit models.




Fig. 1: Macro F1 scores for model settings with a differentiable head.







Fig. 2: Macro F1 scores for model settings with logistic head.



Class-wise performance provides additional insight (Figure 3). In particular, the categories “Mental Health” and “Unspecific” are difficult for the models to predict and strongly influence overall performance. This is also the reason why the baseline model ranks higher than other SetFit configurations, since it achieves higher scores for the harder-to-predict classes, but its performance for the other classes is overall still worse. The unequal class performance may indicate that some categories are too broadly defined or inconsistently annotated. Despite this, overall F1 scores are relatively high, which is encouraging given the complexity of the task.




Fig. 3: Class-wise F1 scores for model settings with logistic head and the baseline.



Training time is a crucial practical factor in active learning, as long delays between iterations disrupt the annotation workflow. As shown in Figure 4, training time largely scales with the number of model parameters. The configuration with the 0.3B e5-base model required the longest training time. In the SetFit framework, training time increases non-linearly because the number of contrastive training pairs grows quadratically with the number of training examples.
For the best-performing SetFit configuration (setfit_paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2_default_CategoryVectorInconsistencyAndRanking), training time increases from roughly 30 seconds with 45 labeled examples to approximately 4 minutes when using the full set of 145 examples. Training the base model took only about two minutes in total.




Fig. 4: Training time per model configuration.

title: Evaluating Active Learning Setups for Qualitative Interview Coding
text:
Concluding Remarks
Based on these experiments, differentiable classification heads do not appear to be a viable option for our use case. While they would offer additional interpretability through token-level attributions, their performance under low-data conditions is insufficient for practical coding workflows.
Among the tested configurations, the paraphrase-based MiniLM sentence transformer stands out as the most suitable “out-of-the-box” choice for our real interview data, combining strong predictive performance with relatively short training times.
For tasks where speedup weighs more heavily than performance, it also seems worth considering the baseline BERT model, since it dramatically reduces training time while the performance drop appears minor at first glance.
As we move to real-world annotation, monitoring class-wise performance and uncertainty estimates will be essential. At the same time, the extent to which a trained model can be interpreted as a reflection of an individual coder’s conceptual understanding remains an open and important question.
Finally, while our experiments cover a broad range of settings, it is possible that relevant configurations were missed. We therefore welcome feedback from others working on similar problems. One promising direction for further experimentation is the multi-label strategy itself, as correlated codes may benefit from approaches beyond the default one-vs-rest formulation.
The code for these experiments is available at: https://github.com/AI-SIC/active-learning-experiments

title: Evaluating ASR for Social Science Research: A Comparison of Semantic Metrics
text:
Planned talk for the ESRA Conference. Shortly, we will publish an article related to our research. For now, you can find the abstract of the talk here.

Abstract
Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) is an essential technology for automating the transcription of qualitative data in social science research, particularly with large interview datasets. Recent advancements in ASR have introduced powerful new tools to the field, but their implementation requires careful and thoughtful consideration to ensure reliability and accuracy. Since outcomes vary significantly depending on the model and its (hyper-)parametrization, it is crucial to evaluate the generalization capabilities of ASR models on specific research data using a meaningful and comparable metric. Addressing these challenges will enable social scientists to effectively leverage these technologies in their research.
The most commonly used metric for this purpose is the Word Error Rate (WER). WER depends on specific language-specific text transformations and focuses on surface-level accuracy, making it inadequate for evaluating transcript quality in social sciences and downstream NLP tasks. To address limitations, modern, semantics-oriented metrics have been developed in recent years. Metrics such as Embedding Error Rate (EmbER) and Semantic-WER apply penalties for different types of errors, while methods like BERTScore, SeMaScore, SemDist, and Aligned Semantic Distance (ASD) improve evaluation by utilizing contextual embeddings and advanced matching techniques to assess semantic similarity.
Our research centers on comparing the usability of these semantic metrics for ASR in social sciences and developing a more intuitive approach for analyzing semantic differences in ASR transcriptions using aligned window-based semantic comparison, as opposed to relying on traditional singular value metrics. The proposed talk is not only designed to improve the quality of individual research projects but also to contribute to the creation of new data spaces for the social sciences, where ASR is a fundamental technology. Only when developing robust methods for evaluating and utilizing ASR, we can unlock the potential of large-scale qualitative datasets, opening up new avenues for research and analysis.

title: Anschreiben
text:
Bitte um Teilnahme an einer Umfrage im Rahmen des wissenschaftlicen Forschungsprojektes AI-SIC
PDF öffnen
Sehr geehrte interessierte Familien,
hiermit möchten wir Sie herzlich einladen, an einer wichtigen wissenschaftlichen Studie zum Thema Gesundheit teilzunehmen. Mit Ihrer Unterstützung helfen Sie uns zu verstehen, wie Kinder und Eltern über Gesundheit sprechen und welche Erfahrungen dabei wichtig sind. Gleichzeitig tragen Sie dazu bei, die Umfrageforschung im Rahmen des Projekts AI-SIC weiterzuentwickeln.
Was ist AI-SIC?
Wir möchten erfahren, wie Kinder und Eltern die Gesundheit von Kindern einschätzen und welche Gedanken oder Erfahrungen dabei eine Rolle spielen. So können wir besser nachvollziehen, was Familien im Zusammenhang mit Kindergesundheit wichtig ist. Wir möchten außerdem die Auswertung der Interviews verbessern und entwickeln dafür computergestützte, teilweise automatisierte Methoden. Diese helfen uns dabei, Antworten schneller und gründlicher auszuwerten. Für unsere wissenschaftliche Forschung brauchen wir Ihre Unterstützung: Mit Ihrer Teilnahme und der Ihres Kindes helfen Sie uns, Forschung über Kinder und Familien weiterzuentwickeln.
Wie sieht die Befragung aus?
Wir möchten mit Ihnen und Ihrem Kind ein kurzes Videogespräch führen. Es findet außerhalb der Schulzeit statt – zum Beispiel am Nachmittag. Die Befragung dauert etwa 20 Minuten für Sie und 10 Minuten für Ihr Kind. Inhaltlich geht es um das Thema Gesundheit. Zusätzlich stellen wir Ihnen einige allgemeine Fragen, zum Beispiel zu Bildung und Herkunft. Das Gespräch wird als Ton (Audio) aufgenommen, damit wir es später sorgfältig auswerten können.
Datenschutz und Umgang mit Ihren Daten
Für das Projekt AI-SIC ist uns der sorgfältige Umgang mit Ihren Daten besonders wichtig. Alle erhobenen Informationen werden gemäß den Vorgaben der Datenschutz-Grundverordnung (DSGVO) streng vertraulich behandelt und ausschließlich für wissenschaftliche Zwecke verwendet. Zudem werden die Daten vor der Analyse anonymisiert, sodass keine Rückschlüsse auf einzelne Personen möglich sind. Weitere Informationen dazu finden Sie im Datenschutzblatt.
Wie können Sie uns konkret unterstützen?
Wenn Sie oder eine andere erziehungsberechtigte Person und Ihr Kind bereit sind, an unserer Studie teilzunehmen, füllen Sie als erziehungsberechtigte Person(en) bitte die Einwilligungs- und Datenschutzerklärung für Eltern aus. Sollte Ihr Kind 13 Jahre oder älter sein, füllt er oder sie bitte zusätzlich die Einwilligungserklärung des Kindes aus; sollte Ihr Kind unter 13 Jahre alt sein, reicht die elterliche Einwilligungserklärung aus. Sie können diese über die Links digital ausfüllen. Selbstverständlich sind Ihre Teilnahme und die Ihres Kindes freiwillig. Bei Nichtteilnahme entstehen Ihnen sowie Ihrem Kind natürlich keinerlei Nachteile.
Dankeschön für Ihre Unterstützung
Die Interviews werden bis mindestens Ende März 2026 durchgeführt. Falls Sie noch Fragen haben, stehen Ihnen Dr. Jacqueline Kroh (jacqueline.kroh@lifbi.de, +49 951 700600-25) und Donata Perakis (donata.perakis@lifbi.de, +49 951 700601-36) gerne zur Verfügung. Wenn Sie sich für eine Teilnahme entscheiden, erhalten Sie im Anschluss an die Befragung als Dankeschön einen Wunschgutschein(www.wunschgutschein.de) im Wert von 10 €. title: Evaluating Active Learning Setups for Qualitative Interview Coding
text:
After completing our preliminary work on transcription, we can now shift focus to the next task: coding our interviews. The aim is to assign labels to interview segments that reflect our dimensions of interest. To align our methodological approach with the needs of our sociological researchers, we decided to use active learning for the labeling process.
Active learning enables human intervention during coding while simultaneously training a machine learning model. Over time, this model can support – and potentially partially automate – the coding process. In this short research notice, we present our findings on different active learning configurations and explain how we identified a suitable setup for our use case.

Test Setting
Active learning refers to an iterative learning setup in which an ML model is trained repeatedly. In each iteration, annotators label examples that are expected to be particularly informative for deciding whether a given label should be assigned. The model is then retrained, and a new batch of examples is selected. The overarching goal is to minimize the total number of labeled examples required.
We implemented our experiments using the small-text active learning framework in Python, which offers a wide range of configuration options.

Data, Annotation, and Evaluation Strategy
Before involving expert coders in annotating the final interview data, we conducted experiments on synthetic interviews to establish baseline practices. These interviews were generated in an AI-to-AI interview setting, where roles, socio-demographic characteristics, and interview guidelines were provided as context.1
From these interviews, we constructed training and test splits. For coding, we selected a small subset of codes that had already been used in a previous study by our team Kroh u. a. (2023).
During data preparation, it became clear that inter-coder agreement would be a central concern for evaluating model performance. A key question is whether a model trained on data labeled by one coder can be meaningfully evaluated on data labeled by another, especially if their interpretations of the codes differ. Even within annotations produced by the same coder, consistency cannot be taken for granted: perceptions of concepts may evolve during the labeling process, and subtle textual differences can lead to different label assignments.
To allow for later analysis of these effects, we tracked which coder labeled each example. For the experiments reported here, we restricted evaluation to a smaller subset of the test data annotated by a single coder, providing a more stable reference point.


Model Architecture and Active Learning Configuration
Turning to the technical setup, our task involves extracting nuanced information from natural language, making transformer-based models a natural choice. Within small-text, two transformer-based approaches are available: a token-level transformer integration (TransformerBasedClassificationFactory) and sentence transformers trained using the SetFit paradigm (SetFitClassificationFactory).
Our experiments focus on sentence transformers, as prior work suggests they outperform the token-based approach in low-data scenarios Tunstall u. a. (2022). Nevertheless, we included one standard transformer model for comparison. Since each interview segment may receive multiple codes, the task is formulated as a multi-label classification problem.
In addition to text representation, several configuration choices can influence model performance. Each model requires a classification head to map embeddings to label predictions. The default option is a logistic regression head implemented in sklearn. As an alternative, we evaluated a differentiable classification head implemented as a linear layer in torch. This option allows for end-to-end training of both the embedding model and the classifier and would later enable the computation of integrated gradients for token-level attribution scores.
For the differentiable head, we tested both full end-to-end training and a setup where embeddings were kept fixed and only the head was trained. Finally, we varied the query strategy that determines which samples are selected for annotation. We compared a prediction-entropy (PE) baseline with the more suitable CategoryVectorInconsistencyAndRanking (CVIAR) strategy, which is designed specifically for multi-label scenarios.
For each configuration, we simulated an active learning run by initializing the model with 20 labeled examples, followed by five iterations in which 25 additional examples were annotated. This resulted in 145 labeled samples per run. The total labeled data pool contained 210 examples, with each configuration selecting different subsets depending on model and query strategy.
We used MLflow to log model configurations, evaluation metrics, training times, and sample selection across iterations. All experiments were run on a SLURM cluster using four Tesla A100 GPUs with 32 GB of memory each, although substantially fewer resources are sufficient when running active learning in a fixed configuration.

title: Evaluating Active Learning Setups for Qualitative Interview Coding
text:
Results
A clear pattern emerges from the results: configurations using a differentiable classification head perform substantially worse than those using a logistic regression head. This is most likely due to the small number of training examples available. Since such low-data conditions are typical in qualitative coding tasks, this finding suggests that differentiable heads are not well suited for our intended application.
Figure 1 summarizes the performance of models using a differentiable head, while Figure 2 shows results for models with a logistic regression head. Performance is evaluated using the macro-averaged F1 score, which balances precision and recall across all codes.
Across almost all settings, the MiniLM model outperforms the newer e5 models – even when compared to the much larger 0.3B-parameter “Medium” variant. The choice of query strategy also has a consistent effect: CategoryVectorInconsistencyAndRanking outperforms entropy-based sampling in nearly every configuration.
Interestingly, the baseline model performed reasonably well against the SetFit models.




Fig. 1: Macro F1 scores for model settings with a differentiable head.







Fig. 2: Macro F1 scores for model settings with logistic head.



Class-wise performance provides additional insight (Figure 3). In particular, the categories “Mental Health” and “Unspecific” are difficult for the models to predict and strongly influence overall performance. This is also the reason why the baseline model ranks higher than other SetFit configurations, since it achieves higher scores for the harder-to-predict classes, but its performance for the other classes is overall still worse. The unequal class performance may indicate that some categories are too broadly defined or inconsistently annotated. Despite this, overall F1 scores are relatively high, which is encouraging given the complexity of the task.




Fig. 3: Class-wise F1 scores for model settings with logistic head and the baseline.



Training time is a crucial practical factor in active learning, as long delays between iterations disrupt the annotation workflow. As shown in Figure 4, training time largely scales with the number of model parameters. The configuration with the 0.3B e5-base model required the longest training time. In the SetFit framework, training time increases non-linearly because the number of contrastive training pairs grows quadratically with the number of training examples.
For the best-performing SetFit configuration (setfit_paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2_default_CategoryVectorInconsistencyAndRanking), training time increases from roughly 30 seconds with 45 labeled examples to approximately 4 minutes when using the full set of 145 examples. Training the base model took only about two minutes in total.




Fig. 4: Training time per model configuration.

title: Evaluating Active Learning Setups for Qualitative Interview Coding
text:
Concluding Remarks
Based on these experiments, differentiable classification heads do not appear to be a viable option for our use case. While they would offer additional interpretability through token-level attributions, their performance under low-data conditions is insufficient for practical coding workflows.
Among the tested configurations, the paraphrase-based MiniLM sentence transformer stands out as the most suitable “out-of-the-box” choice for our real interview data, combining strong predictive performance with relatively short training times.
For tasks where speedup weighs more heavily than performance, it also seems worth considering the baseline BERT model, since it dramatically reduces training time while the performance drop appears minor at first glance.
As we move to real-world annotation, monitoring class-wise performance and uncertainty estimates will be essential. At the same time, the extent to which a trained model can be interpreted as a reflection of an individual coder’s conceptual understanding remains an open and important question.
Finally, while our experiments cover a broad range of settings, it is possible that relevant configurations were missed. We therefore welcome feedback from others working on similar problems. One promising direction for further experimentation is the multi-label strategy itself, as correlated codes may benefit from approaches beyond the default one-vs-rest formulation.
The code for these experiments is available at: https://github.com/AI-SIC/active-learning-experiments

Hintergrund
Um die Qualität der Umfrageforschung zu gewährleisten, werden die Erhebungsinstrumente sowohl mit qualitativen als auch mit quantitativen Methoden validiert. Beide Ansätze sind jedoch mit Einschränkungen verbunden. Während quantitative Analysen aufgrund großer Stichprobengrößen effizient verallgemeinerbare Beziehungen zwischen verschiedenen Konzepten und systematische Unterschiede zwischen den Befragten aufdecken können, sind sie nur begrenzt in der Lage, komplexe kognitive Prozesse innerhalb von Personen zu erfassen.
Im Gegensatz zu quantitativen Methoden bieten qualitative Ansätze wie halbstrukturierte kognitive Interviews tiefere Einblicke in die Denkmuster der Teilnehmer. Die hohen Kosten solcher Studien schränken jedoch häufig die Stichprobengröße und die Skalierbarkeit ein, was die allgemeine Gültigkeit, die Verallgemeinerbarkeit und die Fähigkeit, Unterschiede zwischen Untergruppen zu berücksichtigen, beeinträchtigt.
Die Integration der Stärken beider Methoden kann die Umfrageforschung erheblich verbessern, indem sie ein ganzheitliches Verständnis der Phänomene ermöglicht und gleichzeitig die Vorteile der quantitativen Validierung nutzt. Die Kombination beider Ansätze stellt jedoch eine Herausforderung dar.
Das AI-SIC-Projekt trägt dazu bei, indem es einen KI-basierten Ansatz für halbautomatische Kodierung unter Verwendung einer aktiven Lernstrategie entwickelt. Dabei werden maschinelle Kodieralgorithmen mit menschlichen Kodierfähigkeiten kombiniert. Darüber hinaus werden neue Methoden zur effizienten und gründlichen Validierung von Erhebungsinstrumenten eingesetzt, um Forschungslücken bei der bereits etablierten Messung der selbst eingeschätzten Gesundheit zu schließen. Dies wird dazu beitragen, die Lücke zwischen qualitativen und quantitativen Methoden zu schließen und offene Fragen darüber zu beantworten, wie Kinder und ihre Eltern die Gesundheit von Kindern einschätzen.

Vorgehen und Methoden
Das Projekt ist in vier inhaltliche Arbeitspakete unterteilt.
Das erste Arbeitspaket „Entwicklung des halbautomatischen Kodierframeworks InTraCo “ (Dr. Andreas Niekler & Stephan Poppe; Universität Leipzig) zielt darauf ab, sprachbasiertes maschinelles Lernen und zuverlässige halbautomatische Kodierverfahren methodisch und technisch in den Werkzeugkasten der computergestützten Sozialwissenschaften zu integrieren. Ziel ist es, maschinelle Kodieralgorithmen mit menschlichen induktiven Kodierfähigkeiten zu kombinieren, um die Effizienz bei der Kodierung umfangreicher qualitativer Interviewdaten zu erhöhen.
Das zweite Arbeitspaket „Anwendung und Evaluation von InTraCo “ (Dr. Andreas Niekler & Stephan Poppe; Universität Leipzig) widmet sich der Anwendung des neu entwickelten Ansatzes sowie dessen Validierung und Anpassung.
Das dritte Arbeitspaket „Exploring the self- and proxy-assessment strategies of children and parents “ (Dr. Jacqueline Kroh; LIfBi) nutzt die gewonnenen hochkomplexen Daten und untersucht, ob die neue Methode einen Mehrwert für inhaltsbezogene Analysen mit maschinellen Lernverfahren liefern kann. Damit soll ein umfassenderes Verständnis dafür gewonnen werden, wie Kinder und Eltern die Gesundheit ihrer Kinder einschätzen.

title: Making Implicit Knowledge Explicit: What AI Tools Revealed About Our Coding Scheme
text:
In the project AI-SIC, we aim to analyze qualitative interviews using deductive coding with the help of AI. This includes AI-assisted transcription and semi-automated coding. However, before applying AI to our real interview data, we wanted to address a fundamental question: Is our coding scheme formulated clearly and unambiguously enough to be applied by AI tools?
Through repeated joint review and revision of the coding scheme, we had gradually developed a shared understanding of how to interpret and apply its categories. Yet this process may also have created implicit knowledge: we might take certain rules and distinctions for granted, even though they are not spelled out in the coding scheme itself.
To examine this, we prompted three AI tools (ChatGPT, Claude, and Microsoft 365 Copilot) to code a synthetic interview using the same prompt and our coding scheme. Rather than ranking the tools against each other, we examined their deviations from our human reference coding and the uncertainties they identified. By bringing together these observations, we were able to identify recurring ambiguities, unclear category boundaries, and potential gaps in our coding scheme.
The results indicate that AI tools can serve as an additional perspective in methodological development, helping us identify aspects of our coding scheme that may require further clarification. At the same time, the models differed in how they applied the scheme, so their outputs are best read as pointers rather than a verdict.

title: Making Implicit Knowledge Explicit: What AI Tools Revealed About Our Coding Scheme
text:
Background
At AI-SIC, we conducted semi-structured cognitive interviews with families about children’s self-reported health. Such interviews provide valuable insights but are time-consuming to analyze. A key step in this process is coding: individual text passages are assigned to categories based on a predefined coding scheme.
Our coding scheme distinguishes between 7 analytical categories, containing 34 codes in total. The analytical categories include, among others, the health dimension (which contains codes such as physical, mental, and functional health) and health factors (which contain codes related to more specific health aspects, such as “pain and symptoms,” “acute illnesses,” or “health behaviors”). Other analytical categories include, for example, the temporal context of the statements. A text passage can be assigned multiple codes simultaneously, such as a health factor and the corresponding health dimension. This makes the framework nuanced but also challenging to apply.
Coding therefore is demanding: it requires sustained concentration over long periods and is prone to errors, for example when statements in the interview are ambiguous or the coding scheme does not distinguish clearly enough between different categories.
AI could make coding more efficient. However, reliable AI-assisted coding requires not only a capable model and a well-designed prompt but also a coding scheme whose categories and rules are clear enough that different coders, human or AI, arrive at comparable results.

title: Making Implicit Knowledge Explicit: What AI Tools Revealed About Our Coding Scheme
section: Our Research Interest: Making Implicit Knowledge Explicit
text:
Our Research Interest: Making Implicit Knowledge Explicit
Through repeated joint reviews and revisions of the coding scheme, as well as initial test codings conducted by several team members, we identified areas requiring clarification and revised the scheme several times. During this process, we repeatedly assessed whether the categories were plausible and clearly distinguishable from one another, whether the inclusion and exclusion criteria were precise enough, and whether the examples adequately reflected their respective categories. Through this iterative process, we gradually developed a shared understanding of how to interpret and apply the coding scheme.
However, this shared understanding may also create a blind spot: over time, researchers can develop implicit knowledge of certain distinctions and rules, taking them for granted even when they are not explicitly documented in the coding scheme. They may know, for example, why a particular statement belongs to one category rather than another, whereas someone without this implicit knowledge would make a different coding decision. This raises the question of whether the coding scheme can be understood and applied consistently by coders (whether human or AI tools) who were not involved in its development, based on the written instructions alone.
We used AI tools as an additional perspective to explore this question. Having had no prior involvement in developing the coding scheme, the models could not draw on the shared interpretative understanding established within our research team, although they naturally bring assumptions of their own from training. Their application of the written instructions therefore offered an opportunity to identify potential ambiguities and gaps that might otherwise have remained unnoticed.
Our central research question was: Where do AI tools encounter difficulties when applying our coding scheme, and what do these difficulties reveal about ambiguities or gaps in the scheme itself?
More specifically, we wanted to identify:

Categories whose definitions or boundaries leave room for different interpretations.
Coding rules that are insufficiently explicit or difficult to apply consistently.
Situations in which multiple codes might appear equally plausible.
Concepts or types of statements that are not adequately covered by the existing coding instructions.
Cases in which uncertainty cannot be resolved based on the written coding scheme alone.

Importantly, our aim was not to determine which tool performs best. Instead, we used the combined observations from all models to critically examine our coding scheme. We wanted to find remaining weaknesses and refine the scheme before moving to semi-automated coding, so that both humans and machines can apply it reliably.

title: Making Implicit Knowledge Explicit: What AI Tools Revealed About Our Coding Scheme
text:
Implementation
To conduct the test, we used a synthetic interview from our synthetic dataset (see the article on Silicon Interviews). Although we already have a rich set of original data available, uploading highly sensitive data to commercial web-based AI tools would violate research ethics and data protection regulations. We therefore used a synthetic interview, deliberately chosen because it covered as many different aspects of the scheme as possible: a conversation with “Finn,” a simulated nine-year-old child, which focused, among other things, on how Finn assesses his own health and what health means to him. It contained the same questions as the real interviews and corresponds to an estimated duration of just under 10 minutes (approx. 1,300 words).
In September 2026, we tested our coding scheme with three AI tools: ChatGPT (OpenAI, GPT 5.6 Luna), Claude (Anthropic, Sonnet 5.5), and Microsoft 365 Copilot (based on OpenAI’s GPT 5.6 Sol/Terra/Luna). We compared their output with a human reference coding. ChatGPT and Claude were used with the free standard version of the web interface. Microsoft Copilot was used as a component integrated into the M365 environment. In this environment, we used the default integration of the AI tool with the “auto” setting. This means that, depending on the task at hand, Copilot decides on its own which model to use, choosing between GPT 5.6 Sol, GPT 5.6 Terra, and GPT 5.6 Luna. In a new session, each tool received the same prompt, the coding scheme, and the interview.
The prompt specified the following:

the role of the AI tool,
task, procedure, and workflow,
coding rules, including how to handle uncertainty,
the output format,
a final quality check before output.

We then compared the AI tools’ codings with the human reference coding and brought together all deviations as well as all explicitly reported uncertainties. We treated these observations as potential indicators of unclear definitions, overlapping categories, insufficiently specified decision rules, or missing examples. This approach allowed us to use the tool outputs as a diagnostic instrument for examining the coding scheme itself.

title: Making Implicit Knowledge Explicit: What AI Tools Revealed About Our Coding Scheme
section: Results: What Did the AI Codings Reveal About Our Coding Scheme?
text:
Results: What Did the AI Codings Reveal About Our Coding Scheme?
The analysis revealed several recurring areas in which the tools’ interpretations differed from our human reference coding or in which the models explicitly expressed uncertainty. These cases pointed to aspects of the coding scheme that may require further clarification.

1. Health Behavior or Functional Capacity? Why the Meaning of an Activity Matters
One recurring issue concerned the distinction between health behavior and functional capacity. For example, consider Finn’s statement “I’m always outside playing soccer, jumping on the trampoline.” The statement describes an activity that could be interpreted in two ways. It might represent health behavior, because physical activity is generally associated with health. Alternatively, it might describe functional capacity in leisure activities, because Finn emphasizes what he is able to do. The reference coding primarily assigned the statement to functional capacity in leisure activities. Health behavior was considered a possible but less likely alternative. The outputs of the AI tools reflected this ambiguity: different interpretations emerged, and one model explicitly identified both categories as potentially applicable. The coding scheme therefore needs to clarify what distinguishes health-promoting behavior from the ability to perform activities. Is the intention behind an activity decisive? Does the statement need to explicitly describe an activity as something done to maintain health? Or is the activity itself sufficient? Without clearer decision rules, the same statement can plausibly be assigned to different categories.


2. Feeling Fit: Which Health Dimension and Health Factor Is It?
Another recurring issue concerned statements such as “I feel strong and fit.” In our reference coding, “feeling fit” was primarily classified as the nonspecific health dimension, because it is not immediately clear whether this refers to physical or mental fitness. The AI tools also considered physical health as a possible health dimension. This points to a possible need to revise the nonspecific category. With regard to the health factor as well, it became apparent that “being fit” was a borderline case: in the reference coding it was classified as subjective well-being (affect/well-being), while the AI tools also considered health-related resources as a possible assignment. This hints at an unclear boundary between these two health factors, which clearer guidelines would have to resolve.


3. Sleep, Tiredness, and Feeling Rested: An Unclear Conceptual Boundary
Similar to “feeling fit”, sleep-related statements revealed another area of uncertainty. Consider statements such as “I wake up feeling rested”, “I would be tired all day” or “I sleep well and get enough rest”. Depending on the context, these statements could describe health behavior, health-related resources, or affect/well-being. Tiredness might also be interpreted as a symptom. The outputs of the AI tools reflected these different possibilities. In particular, the distinction between sleep as a behavior and sleep as a health-related state was not consistently clear. The uncertainty notes also highlighted that tiredness was not explicitly assigned to a sufficiently clear category in the coding scheme. The scheme would benefit from an explicit rule on how sleep-related experiences, including tiredness, are coded.


4. When Should Multiple Codes Apply?
Further uncertainties arose in the assignment of parallel codes. Notable differences emerged at various points in the interview: While some AI tools, for example, selected a single health factor, others coded multiple health factors simultaneously for the same statement. The example from point 1, “I’m always outside playing soccer, jumping on the trampoline.”, was coded by one of the AI tools as health behavior and also as functional capacity in leisure activities. Evidently, the rules for parallel coding need to be more specific: when is a second code justified, and when should coders commit to a single one?


5. What Exactly Is Being Quantified?
Finally, several statements revealed uncertainties about the application of our quantification code (captures the prevalence of diseases/pain and symptoms, or of positive conditions). Expressions such as “hardly ever”, “only for a few days”, or “every morning” can refer to frequency, duration or regularity of said conditions. It raises the question of whether the regularity or duration of symptoms, conditions, or diseases should also be included in the quantification code. This suggests that the scope and application of the quantification code should be reviewed.

title: Making Implicit Knowledge Explicit: What AI Tools Revealed About Our Coding Scheme
section: Lessons Learned: Using AI Tools for Methodological Development
text:
Lessons Learned: Using AI Tools for Methodological Development
The pretest indicates that AI tools can provide a useful additional perspective when reviewing a qualitative coding scheme. The most valuable insights emerged from examining recurring deviations and uncertainties across the different outputs.
Three broader lessons stand out:

1. Shared Team Knowledge Is Not Necessarily Documented Knowledge
The AI tools highlighted distinctions that seemed relatively straightforward to our research team but were not always sufficiently explicit in the written coding instructions. This reinforced our starting concern: a shared understanding among researchers is no substitute for fully operationalized coding rules.


2. Ambiguities Cluster at Conceptual Boundaries
Many of the identified issues were not a matter of wording. They touched on fundamental conceptual boundaries, such as health behavior versus functional capacity. In some cases, the underlying decision rules and definitions may therefore need to be rethought, not just clarified.


3. Different Interpretations Can Be a Starting Point for Discussion, Not Necessarily an Indication of an Error
A deviation from the reference coding does not automatically mean that an AI tool has made a mistake. It can also reveal that a particular statement permits multiple plausible interpretations or that the coding scheme does not sufficiently specify how to resolve a borderline case. Therefore, all identified deviations and uncertainties need to be reviewed by the research team before changes are made.

title: Making Implicit Knowledge Explicit: What AI Tools Revealed About Our Coding Scheme
text:
Conclusion & Outlook
Our pretest offers first indications that AI tools can be useful not only for applying an existing coding scheme but also for critically examining and improving it. By asking several AI tools to code the same synthetic interview, we identified recurring ambiguities and potential gaps in our coding instructions. These included the distinction between health behavior and functional capacity, the interpretation of subjective feelings of being fit and the classification of sleep and tiredness.
The key insight is that AI tools can help us make implicit knowledge explicit. Their interpretations provide an additional perspective that is not shaped by the shared understanding developed within our research team.
Our findings come with limitations. We tested only one synthetic interview of about ten minutes, with one run per tool and a single prompt. Synthetic interviews may not fully capture how real children and parents speak, and the output of AI tools can vary from run to run. We therefore regard the results as pointers for further review rather than as evidence of specific flaws in the scheme.
Our next step is to systematically review the identified borderline cases, discuss them internally, and decide which ones point to genuine weaknesses in the coding scheme. We will then revise the relevant definitions, inclusion and exclusion criteria, and illustrative examples.
Ultimately, we want to ensure that our coding scheme can be applied consistently by both human researchers and AI tools by making the underlying coding rules sufficiently transparent and explicit. Our preliminary conclusion is that AI tools can serve as a valuable aid for quality assurance and methodological reflection, helping researchers identify what their coding scheme still leaves open. Using synthetic data and multiple tools is helpful, as is having the tools identify their uncertainties and treat discrepancies as opportunities for discussion.

title: What Does a Machine Learn? Experiments on Concept Representations of Human Coders and Machine Learning Models
text:
One goal of our research project is to develop a coding tool that helps researchers scale up the labor-intensive task of coding. We approach this with active learning, a machine learning paradigm that iteratively involves human coders in model training: they decide on the boundary cases that are most informative for the model, so that it learns the human definition of the codes as efficiently as possible. After each feedback round, the model is retrained on the newly coded examples and, based on what it has learned so far, selects the next most informative examples from the pool of uncoded material (see our article on active learning setups). This process rests on a crucial assumption: that the human coder holds a coherent understanding of a code that someone else, be it another coder or a model, can adopt. Since this assumption also determines what “scaling up coding” can accomplish, we took the time to investigate, in an experiment with multiple coders, how the coders’ understandings of the codes relate to each other and to the representation a model learns from them. To make this comparison, we used explainable AI (XAI) methods to identify the parts of an interview passage that are relevant to the model’s prediction. This article briefly summarizes our findings.
The experiments are part of the author’s master’s thesis, which develops the methodological groundwork for this comparison: it examines how the representation a model learns from coded examples can be related to human interpretations of a code, and how XAI can be used to surface ambiguity in coding rather than conceal it. Here, we report only the observations most relevant to our work at AI-SIC; a more detailed publication will follow.

title: What Does a Machine Learn? Experiments on Concept Representations of Human Coders and Machine Learning Models
text:
Experimental Setup
To compare the model with the human coders, we needed to make their understanding of a code empirically comparable. We did this by tracing it back to the coded interview passages, highlighting the words that were important for a coding decision. Such highlights can be obtained from the human coders as well as, by means of XAI, from the classification model, and since both refer to the same passages, they can be compared directly. Although highlights are only an abstract proxy for the understanding of a code, our qualitative readings showed that in many cases they supported a coherent reading of it.
Our experiments draw on the first batch of 54 fully transcribed and anonymized cognitive interviews. As this was a preliminary study rather than our full coding, we restricted the analysis to selected questions from our interview guideline and to a limited set of codes: the health dimensions (“physical”, “functional”, “mental”) and the reference criteria (“social”, “intrapersonal”, “normative”) (Kroh u. a. 2023). We located the relevant questions in the transcripts using a simple approach based on regular expressions.
After preprocessing, this left us with 281 respondent answers, which we split into a training set (221) and a test set (60). The training set was coded exclusively by the author of this article, who is referred to as the trainer in the following (annotator 1 in the figures), and served to train the classification model. The test set was coded by four project members, again including the author. In a first coding phase, each of them assigned one or more codes to every example and rated how certain they were of each assignment on a scale from 1 (very uncertain) to 10 (very certain) (see Fig. 1).
In a second phase, each coder was shown their own coding decisions again and asked to highlight the parts of the passage that had been relevant to each assignment (see Fig. 2).







Fig. 1: First coding phase in Argilla: coders assign codes for both dimensions and rate their certainty for each assigned code.











Fig. 2: Second coding phase in Argilla: coders highlight the parts of the passage that were relevant to their assignment.




The human coding alone already tells us a lot about how the coders understand the codes: we can derive agreement scores for individual codes, relate them to the coders’ certainty ratings, and trace disagreements back to possibly divergent readings. To obtain comparable evidence on the model side, we used the XAI method Integrated Gradients (Sundararajan u. a. 2017). It assigns each word of a passage an attribution score that indicates whether, and how strongly, the word pushed the model towards or away from a code.1 For every test example, this gives us the model’s prediction, its probability for each code, and word-level attributions, the latter even for codes where the model’s probability stayed below the 0.5 threshold.

title: What Does a Machine Learn? Experiments on Concept Representations of Human Coders and Machine Learning Models
text:
Findings

The Human Side
Since the highlights were tied to the coding decisions, agreement among the coders on a code was a prerequisite for comparing them. In this respect, the experiments also turned out to be an insightful pre-test for our actual coding, as they showed that we did not interpret all codes uniformly.2 As Tab. 1 shows, agreement varies considerably between the codes: it is highest for “Physical Health” and “Social Reference”, the latter, however, being rarely assigned, and lowest for “Intrapersonal Reference” and “Normative Reference”. As the reference criteria were assigned rarely or with low agreement, the model-side analysis focuses on the three health codes.

One reason for these mixed results lies in single coders whose understanding of a code deviated from that of the others: this happened for three codes, each time with a different coder. The UpSet plot in Fig. 3 (a) shows this for “Mental Health”: annotator 1, the trainer, assigned the code to 8 passages where none of the other coders did. In these cases, the trainer counted rather general descriptions of health as mental health, since the codebook contained an ambiguous example for such cases. An average certainty of 3.375 for these assignments indicates that the trainer was unsure about them as well. Similar patterns can be observed for “Intrapersonal Reference” and “Normative Reference”. The latter was almost exclusively assigned by one coder: in 11 of the 13 cases in which this coder assigned it, no one else did (Fig. 3 (b)). This time, however, the coder was confident in the divergent reading, with an average certainty of 8.23.

Fig. 3: Coder agreement on “Mental Health” and “Normative Reference”. Each bar counts the passages to which exactly the combination of coders marked by the dots below assigned the code; the bars on the left show how often each coder assigned it in total.



This leads to our first lesson: coding is a cognitively demanding task that involves at least two layers: understanding what a code means, and deciding whether a passage meets it. Vague formulations in the codebook can create uncertainty in the latter and, as a consequence, disagreement between coders. But even when coders are certain in their decisions, their understandings of what a code means may still differ.


The Model Side
On the model side, we wanted to know how the coders’ divergent interpretations relate to the representation the model learns from the coded examples. As the model was trained on examples coded by the trainer alone, the first question was how far this shapes its representation compared to the other coders. Put simply: is the model a puppet of its trainer, or can it infer a more general representation of a code from the training examples? Our experiments point towards the former. When we ranked the coders by how closely their highlights matched the model’s positive attributions, the trainer ranked closest to the model on average for each of the three health codes.3
Fig. 4 shows a case in which this lean becomes visible. All four coders assigned “Mental Health” to the passage, but while the other coders highlighted only “seelisches Wohlbefinden” (mental well-being) as relevant, the trainer additionally highlighted “Motivation mich zu bewegen” (motivation to get moving). Another finding that shows in this example is the importance of key terms that trigger a code assignment. The positive attributions are distributed very unevenly: “Motivation” receives a score of +1.85, about three times as much as the third-highest word. “Seelisches” also scores high, and it is arguably the term that carries the consistent assignment of the code across all coders and the model in this case. Across codes, this concentration is most pronounced for “Physical Health”, where the highest-scoring word alone accounts for 41% of a passage’s positive attribution on average. The same code also showed the highest agreement among the coders and the closest match between human highlights and model attributions. In contrast, where the trainer was uncertain about an assignment, the model’s attributions were spread more evenly across the passage (Fig. 5).4

These general trends were complemented by a close reading, which showed that, read across multiple examples, the attributions could in some cases be assembled into a coherent reading of the model’s representation of a code. For instance, terms related to everyday activities, such as playing, doing sports and going to school, received high attribution scores for “Functional Health” across several examples. However, this is a selective reading that may not hold for other cases. The attributions were also not always interpretable: in some cases, relatively high scores could not be brought into any coherent reading.
This leads to our second lesson, which can be summarized in three points:

Model predictions always have to be considered in light of the interpretation carried by the training examples.
Uncertainty in interpretation and ambiguity in the data are also reflected in the model’s representation of a code.
To some extent, IG attributions can make this representation accessible.

title: What Does a Machine Learn? Experiments on Concept Representations of Human Coders and Machine Learning Models
section: What Does This Mean for the AI-SIC Project?
text:
What Does This Mean for the AI-SIC Project?
In our use case, the coding of cognitive interviews, we aim to minimize ambiguity, as our codes serve to ground statements about empirical relationships in the data. Nonetheless, some ambiguity is unavoidable when applying abstract codes to diverse interview material, since this is always an interpretive act. As a consequence of the experiments, we revised our codebook and now brief our coders in order to reduce the room for interpretation wherever possible. In this setting, XAI attributions can serve as an intermediate quality check after several rounds of training, verifying that the model has picked up the right cues before it is applied to unseen material.
In other forms of social science coding, such as Grounded Theory, ambiguity is embraced as a productive part of the coding itself. Here, XAI attributions could be used in a more interactive human–machine setting to surface the ambiguity in the learned representation, for example by deliberately reviewing cases with diffuse attributions or by reading attributions across assignments. Confronting this ambiguity could then push researchers to rethink their own categories.
In both cases, however, our experiments show that attributions can be misleading when used as a decision aid (Miller 2023), as they themselves carry various kinds of ambiguity and are error-prone when read for a single case. Their intended use is therefore not to justify individual model decisions, for instance as a coding helper that tells coders why a code applies, but to support extended reasoning about the codebook and the modeling process across many cases.

title: Transcribing Children’s Health Interviews with AI: What Worked, What Didn’t
text: Qualitative interviews are a rich data source, but turning audio into analyzable text is time-consuming and labor-intensive. Automatic speech recognition (ASR) models promise to automate this step. Yet many tools exist, and many challenges remain, especially for sensitive data and non-standard speech (see our article on ASR evaluation). In the project AI-SIC, we develop an efficient framework to transcribe and code qualitative data using different machine learning methods. This post reports on another output of the project: our experience transcribing qualitative interviews with AI and correcting the results by hand.

title: Transcribing Children’s Health Interviews with AI: What Worked, What Didn’t
text:
The data
We worked with 96 German-language interviews on children’s health stemming from cognitive interviews with both children (aged 8–16) and their parents. Parents were asked about their overall assessment of their children’s health, medical diagnoses and illnesses the child had in the past, and socio-demographic characteristics of themselves and of the child. Additionally, we also asked children about their own health assessment and perception of health. The interviews took around 30 minutes in total and were recorded with separate audio channels for the interviewer and the participants, as well as a joint one. The recording strategy turned out to be a crucial factor (see below).

title: Transcribing Children’s Health Interviews with AI: What Worked, What Didn’t
text:
Our approach in brief
Our approach is split into two parts:

The technical pipeline. We used NVIDIA NeMo (Kuchaiev u. a. 2019) for automatic speaker diarization and Whisper Turbo (Radford u. a. 2023) with a prompt for automatic speech recognition, as well as wav2vec 2.0 (Baevski u. a. 2020) for the timestamp alignment. A preliminary fine-tuning experiment with data from kidsTALC (Rumberg u. a. 2022) (University of Hannover) showed no significant improvement for our use case and was therefore not utilized. The entire pipeline, including preprocessing, transcription, timestamp alignment, speaker diarization, merging and exporting the results, took approximately 1–2 minutes per interview (compute time). A subsequent quality check revealed errors in both speaker diarization and text transcription, making manual correction necessary.
The manual correction. We chose the subtitle software Aegisub because it is free, has an accessible interface (Figure 1), supports various audio formats, and makes text and speaker corrections easy. Student assistants did the correction after training and with detailed step-by-step instructions.
We applied four correction steps and saved a separate version of the transcript after each stage, so the process can be evaluated afterwards:

Step 1, speaker assignment: Statements were reassigned where the model attributed them to the wrong person. Where overlapping audio caused a statement to be missed entirely, it was added manually.
Step 2, text correction: Wrongly transcribed words and sentences were corrected.
Step 3, pseudonymization: Information that could identify participants was removed or changed. This step was the most demanding as researchers must remove identifying information without altering the meaning of a statement or deleting context needed for analysis. We replaced first names, last names and street names with randomly chosen entries from lists of 20 alternatives (separate lists for male, female, children’s and adults’ first names). Specific school names were removed, leaving only the type of school (e.g., “Martin Luther elementary school” became “[elementary school]”). Further details, such as those regarding specific diagnoses and disease progression, had to be coordinated within the team to ensure pseudonymization tailored to each individual case.
Step 4, merging lines: Consecutive lines by the same speaker were merged into one line per statement.






Fig. 1: Screenshot of the Aegisub interface.

title: Transcribing Children’s Health Interviews with AI: What Worked, What Didn’t
text:
What we learned

1. Speaker recognition and transcription quality pull in opposite directions

Joint recording: Speaker recognition was moderate to poor, depending on the voices. When interviewer and participant had similar voices (e.g., two women with rather high voices), the assigned speaker sometimes changed within a sentence, even repeatedly (Figure 2). With clearly different voices, recognition worked better.
Separate tracks: Speaker recognition was almost perfect, but the transcript itself got considerably worse, containing more misunderstood words, missing passages, and hallucinations. Therefore, we assume that the dialog context improves transcription quality, which is missing in the separate tracks. Compiling the transcripts of the separate tracks into a combined transcript also appeared problematic as the timestamps were not reliable enough for the task: Due to shifts and lack of separation in the timestamps, the compilation resulted in the sequence of the conversation no longer matching the audio. This was most visible in the questions on illnesses, where interviewer and participant alternated quickly with short answers. In the combined transcripts from the separate tracks, these passages often showed wrongly grouped short answers (Figure 3) instead of the rapid question-answer exchanges or just added the answer to the next question (Figure 4). With the given timestamp precision this problem was impossible to resolve, as it constituted a trade-off between wrongly grouped short passages and wrongly separated speech acts depending on the defined pause duration.





Fig. 2: Change in speaker assignment during the same statement.







Fig. 3: Errors in the interview transcript due to rapid changes in speakers.







Fig. 4: Fast replies added to the next question.





2. Audio quality still decides
Some problems appeared in both versions. Paraverbal utterances such as “Mhm” or “Hmm” were transcribed inconsistently and background noise as well as connection problems partly led to wrong or missing words. Dialects were recognized very well, and accents (e.g., from a different first language) caused problems in rather few cases. Some medical terms were replaced with similar-sounding words (e.g., “Eitrige Bindehautentzündung”, “Blasen- und Harnwegsinfekt”), but only when they were pronounced quickly or unclearly.


3. Pseudonymization is harder with health data and a non-human coder
Because the interviews were about health, preventing re-identification was especially important. At the same time, diseases are the core of our research interest. Rare diseases carry a high re-identification risk, but replacing them with “[disease]” would cause a major loss of information. The same holds for rare hobbies or sports, which give important context for how participants assess their child’s health. We also had to reflect on how the pseudonymization would affect machine learning classifiers further down the line. While it might be possible to anticipate human coders’ needs, this is much harder and unresearched for coding by an active learner. Due to those complexities, in 29 of the 96 interviews, a simple pseudonymization was not possible, and the team had to discuss how to handle the passage. We follow Qualiservice’s recommendations (Mozygemba und Hollstein 2026) and classify such health conditions under the higher-level categories of the ICD-10.


4. The human side: faster, but demanding
For the people correcting, model-based transcription saved considerable time compared to manual transcription. Still, detailed correction required high concentration and precision, which led to fatigue and the need for breaks and task changes. Overall, the correction took two to four hours per interview, depending on the length and complexity of corrections and the experience of the correctors. Correcting one’s own interviews can sometimes be faster, but listening to one’s own voice for a long time was perceived as irritating.

title: Transcribing Children’s Health Interviews with AI: What Worked, What Didn’t
text:
Conclusion and recommendations
Two findings stand out. First, we recognized a trade-off: separate audio tracks improve speaker recognition but remove context that the model needs for accurate transcription and additionally introduce the challenge to recombine them properly. Second, audio quality strongly determines transcript quality. Overlapping speech, background noise, poor connections, and strong accents make human correction indispensable.
For researchers using a similar approach, we suggest:

Avoid passages with rapid exchanges or long rows of quick yes/no questions.
Use prompts for transcription models to condition the model on the desired transcription style as a cheap alternative to complex fine-tunings with unpredictable outcome (see e.g. the Whisper prompting guide).
Prioritize a recording with separate audio channels only in case speaker diarization is your major concern. If the content is more important, a joint recording with manual post-correction of the speakers is more manageable.

title: Evaluating Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) for Social Science Research: A Comparison of Semantic Metrics
text:
Semantic Metrics
In general, we can identify two ways to obtain more meaningful metrics. The first way is to improve the word error rate by weighting different classes of errors differently. For example, we could assign higher error penalties when nouns are incorrectly transcribed and lower penalties when articles are incorrect.
Instead of this approach, there are also metrics that move away from measuring lexical errors altogether. These use so-called word embeddings to compare whether the reference and hypothesis align semantically.
We will discuss one representative from each group to get a better sense of what they can tell us about transcription quality. It is worth noting that we set up these meta-categories to better understand what the metrics do, but the different representatives within these categories still share common principles, such as alignment and embedding strategies.

Weighted WER
A good example of the weighted WER is the Semantic-WER by Roy (2021). It uses a sophisticated ruleset for each of the WER error types (Substitution, Deletion, Insertion). This formula is taken from Roy (2021) page 2:


W_{\text{sub}} =
\begin{cases}
{1,} & {\text{if } r_w \in \text{NE} \cup \text{SENT}} \\
\text{cer}(r_w, h_w), & \text{if } r_w \in \text{SE} \\
\dots &\\
\end{cases}


Just looking at one of these rulesets for substitutions, we can see that different kinds of words are assigned different error weights. If the reference word (r_w) substituted by another word was a named entity (NE) or a sentiment word (SENT), an error of 1 is assigned. This rule, for example, ensures that substitution of place names such as “London” contributes to a higher overall error.
The second case accounts for spelled-out entities (SE), for example in telephone interviews, where we compute how many characters are incorrect using the character error rate between reference and hypothesis (cer(r_w, h_w)).
The list goes on, but from here the idea should be clear. Another simpler way to weigh errors is used by the Embedding Error Rater (EmbER) by Roux u. a. (2022), which weighs errors by distance in embedding space.


Semantically based Error Rates
Moving away from comparison based on alignment at the lexical level, the BERTScore by Zhang u. a. (2020) first embeds every single token of the reference and hypothesis using a BERT encoder. This approach leverages the idea that in the embedding space, similar words tend to be closer to each other. Similarity is assumed to be reflected across multiple dimensions—not only lexical or grammatical ones.
For example, in the following projection of an embedding space, the relationship between countries and their capitals is reflected, along with some notion of geographical proximity.




Word Embeddings Concept. Source: https://lovit.github.io/assets/figures/word2vec_country_capital.png.



After obtaining the embedding vectors, BERTScore aligns reference and hypothesis tokens based on proximity in embedding space. Then, token-based cosine similarity is used to compute a similarity score between aligned tokens. This similarity is weighted by TF-IDF (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency) to give more importance to terms that are more characteristic of the document.
This idea is also employed by several other metrics that differ slightly in implementation. The Semantic Distance (SemDist) by Kim u. a. (2021) uses sentence-level embeddings. The Aligned Semantic Distance (ASD) by Rugayan u. a. (2023) applies character-level alignment and weighs edit-level errors by semantic proximity of segments. The SeMaScore by Sasindran u. a. (2024) uses dynamic programming for alignment, proceeding in a similar way as ASD. These are just a few examples highlighting key differences in semantic error metrics.

title: Evaluating Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) for Social Science Research: A Comparison of Semantic Metrics
section: Our proposal: Visually aided Semantic Evaluation
text:
Our proposal: Visually aided Semantic Evaluation
After reviewing various error metrics, the key question remains: can they truly help us evaluate transcription models for our specific needs? While it’s valuable to assess transcripts beyond just lexical accuracy—and combining different metrics can reveal the types of errors—looking at scores aggregated over an entire transcript only gives a general, averaged picture. It doesn’t show us where or how the errors happen throughout the interview.
To overcome this limitation and give researchers deeper insight into transcript quality, we developed a notebook that tracks errors over time—that is, across the length of the transcript.




Our proposal: Interactive analysis of errors (Screenshot). Full code under: https://github.com/ai-sic/semantic-asr-evaluation.



Specifically, we chunk a transcript into segments and measure the error for each segment based on similarity in embedding space. This approach enables interactive investigation of how errors vary throughout the transcript. It also helps identify problematic parts of the data.
In the example figure, the first part of the transcript is missing, which could be caused by poor audio quality or background noise during that segment.
